name: Secret Societies
fwnote: Codes are the Illinois Learning Standards for Social Science by strand (IS inquiry skills; CV civics; EC economics; G geography; H history) and by grade (K-5), band (6-8, with LC/MdC/MC complexity levels) or 9-12. The course weighs claims about secret societies against the historical record, so it cites history, civics and inquiry standards; alignment is the course author's judgment and not a certification.

1.bq: How can clubs and secrets be kind, fair and safe?
std: SS.CV.2.K
Explain why rules are needed and what they are for at school and elsewhere
SS.CV.1.1
Explain that everyone in a community, not only leaders, has an important role
SS.IS.6.K-2
Use listening, consensus and voting to make decisions and act together in class
1.write: Draw or write about a club you would make. What is its name and symbol? Write one fair rule. Then tell one secret your club could keep, and say why it is a safe secret.

ch.bq: What makes a club a good place to belong?
ch.talk: The friends made a rule for new kids. What rule would you make for your club? Why?

l.look: What does each table share? Which table would you like to sit at?
Which sign is a hobby? Which is a team? Which would you pick?
What is the symbol on this badge? Draw a badge for a club you would like.
Which rule keeps things fair? Which rule would you add?
What did Ana do to welcome him? What else could she do?
How does the third child feel in each picture? Which answer is kind?
Count up with your finger. Where are the club rooms? Why do you think a club wanted a big building?
Who did Mooseheart help? How did club members help children they had never met?

ch.bq: How can I tell which secrets to keep and which secrets to tell?
ch.talk: How did Eli feel while he kept the card a secret? How is that different from a scary feeling?

l.t: A Surprise Is a Happy Secret
l.look: Is this a happy secret? How do you think the brother will feel when he opens it?
When will this surprise end? How will the girl feel on Saturday?
Why did the builders ask questions? Is a secret word like this safe or unsafe?
Which drawing shows an unsafe secret? What clues did you see on his face?
Why do you think Illinois wants every child to learn this?
Who would go on the fingers of your helping hand?
Which one can kids fix? Which one needs a grown-up right away?

l.t: Keep Telling Until You Get Help
l.look: What did the girl do when her aunt was busy? What would you do?

2.bq: How do pictures, codes and secret words help a group share ideas?
std: Explain how documents, objects, pictures and oral accounts can be used to study the past
SS.H.1.K
Compare how people lived in the past with how they live today
SS.CV.2.1
Identify rules and explain how they work in different settings in and out of school
2.write: Think about codes and passwords. Are they a good thing for a club to have? Tell or write your answer. Use two things you learned, like the pigpen code, the builders' password or safe secrets.

ch.bq: How can a picture tell us something without any words?
ch.talk: Have you seen a picture on a wall or a sign that made you wonder what it meant? What did you think it said?
ch.story: The Picture on the Old Building

l.look: Say what each picture means. Which one would you put on a card for a friend?
Which sign has the most sides? Draw that shape in the air with your finger.
How many steps does the floor show? Why might a group show its steps in pictures?
Which tool makes corners? Which tool draws circles? Show each shape with your hands.
Pick one carving. What could it tell you about the building?
Which number is the biggest? What does each star stand for?
What does your class love? Draw a simple picture that shows it.

ch.bq: How does a code work, and when is a secret OK to keep?
ch.talk: Why could Lucy read the note but Leo could not? What made this a happy secret?

l.look: Read the name in the note. Now write your own name with numbers.
Which friends can read a note in star, moon and sun? How could the third friend join the game?
How many letters go in the two grids? How many go in the two X shapes?
What two kinds of symbols are on the stone? How can a person read the pigpen line?
Why would builders want to test what a new worker remembered?
Make up one hand signal for your class. What message will it give?
Which secrets are happy? Which one is unsafe and must be told to a grown-up?
Who are five grown-ups you could tell if a secret felt unsafe?

3.bq: How did builders and helpers make their towns stronger?
std: SS.EC.2.1
Describe the skills and knowledge needed to produce particular goods and services
SS.CV.2.2
Describe how a community works together on shared tasks and assigns roles and responsibilities
Summarize how the local community has changed over time
3.write: Were lodges good helpers for their towns? Tell or write your answer. Use two things you learned, like the lodge doctor, Mooseheart or the Shriners hospital.

ch.bq: How did builders long ago make giant stone churches by hand?
ch.talk: If you had your own mark to carve on your work, what would it look like? Why would you pick that shape?

l.look: Who do you think cut and stacked all these stones? Point to the part that would be hardest to build.

l.t: Built by Hand, Year by Year
l.look: Which church took the longest to build? Which one was the fastest?
Which stack will fall first? Which tool would a builder use to fix the bottom block?

l.t: The Plumb Line and the Mallet
l.look: Does the side of the door match the string? Try it with a string and a washer at home or in class.
What is one thing you learned step by step, like riding a bike? Who helped you?
How many builders do you think cut these stones? Draw a mark you could use on your own work.

s.t: The Lodge at the Building Site

l.look: Which rule would help a team of builders the most? Which rule could your class use?
Why would builders want to know a new worker was really trained?

ch.bq: How can a club help its members and its neighbors?
ch.talk: How did the lodge help Rosa's family? Who helps your family when things are hard?

l.look: Why is it good that everyone puts in a little? What could your class save up for together?
How do you think Rosa feels when the doctor comes? Why?
What would a child need in a town like this? Name three things.
Which of these began first? Which began last?
What club is this? What does the sign tell you about what they do?
What year did the Chicago hospital open? Who helped build it?
Which building has the most floors? How many more floors did the Masonic Temple have than the Home Insurance Building?
Which club acts like a kind club? What would you do if a club said the second thing?

4.t: Mystery Rites of the Ancient World
4.bq: How can we learn the truth about ancient groups that worked hard to keep their secrets?
std: Build and use a timeline of related events to compare developments of the same period
Find sources with multiple points of view to help answer essential questions
Judge how useful a historical source is by its maker, date, origin, audience and purpose
4.write: Which group kept its secrets better: the initiates of Eleusis, the followers of Mithras, or the Pythagoreans? Make a claim. Use two or three facts or sources from this unit to support it, and explain your thinking.

ch.bq: How did thousands of people keep one secret for more than a thousand years?
ch.talk: Why do you think Melissa kept her promise, even when her friends asked her what happened?

s.t: A Holy Place and Its Story

l.look: About how far was Eleusis from Athens? Name a place about that far from your school.
Which picture matches the time Persephone is with her mother? Explain how the myth fits the seasons.

l.t: The Hymn That Tells the Story
l.look: What does the hymn promise to people who have seen the rites? Why might that make someone want to join?
Using the rules in the reading, which of these three people could begin the Mysteries? Explain your answer.
What would you hear, see and feel on this walk? How might walking together change how people felt about each other?
Why do you think the list of things we do not know is about the most secret part of the night?
Which questions could Nikias answer, and which one must he keep secret? Use the reading to explain.
Pausanias describes many temples in detail. Why does he stop here? What does that tell you about the secret?
What can you learn from this picture? What is still hidden?

s.t: Why People Came, and the End

l.look: Which friend is talking about hope for the afterlife? Which one is talking about belonging? Which reason matters more to you?
Which event happened longest ago? About how many years passed between the tablet being given and being found?

ch.bq: How can we learn about a secret group that left almost no writing of its own?
ch.talk: The team almost missed the head because it was the last day. What does this story tell you about how archaeology works?
ch.story: The Last Day of the Dig

l.look: The two torches point in opposite directions. What might up and down stand for? Remember that nobody knows for sure.
How is this room different from a big temple with columns in the sunlight? Why might a small group want a room like this?
Tertullian was a Christian writer who did not like this religion. What does his story tell us? Why should we read it with care?
Which layer is the oldest? Why does the oldest layer end up at the bottom?
Why might a group put its ranks on the floor, where members walk over them? What would that feel like?
Name your seven steps and draw a symbol for each. What would someone learn at each step?
About how many years passed between when the temple was built and when the head was found?
Trace the trip with your finger. Why might a teacher move to a new city to start a group?
These rules sound strange. Many people think some were meant as picture-sayings with hidden meanings. What might do not stir a fire with a knife mean?
Add the first two numbers. What do you get? Try it with sides 6, 8 and 10.

l.t: What We Know and What We Were Told
l.look: Sort the cards into two piles: well supported, or legend. Explain one choice using the reading.

5.bq: How can we tell what really happened to the Knights Templar from the legends people tell about them?
std: Explain historical contexts and why groups in the same period held different perspectives
Judge how useful a historical source is by its maker, date, origin, audience and purpose
Explain likely causes and effects of events and developments in U.S. history
5.write: Were the Templars guilty of the charges against them? Write a paragraph that answers the question. Use two or three facts or sources from this unit, such as the confessions, the Chinon Parchment or the pope's 1312 decision. Explain how each one supports your answer.

ch.bq: How did a small group of knights guarding pilgrims grow into one of the richest groups in Europe?
ch.talk: Why might Pierre feel safer carrying a piece of paper than a bag of coins? What would he need to trust?

l.look: What dangers do you see on this road? What would help these travelers feel safe?

l.t: Hugh of Payns Starts a Brotherhood
l.look: How many years after the Christians took Jerusalem did the Templars begin? Show how you figured it out.
William wrote about 50 years after 1118. Which part of his story would you want to check against other records? Why?
Pick one classroom rule. What problem does it solve? What problem might a rule about meals or clothing solve for a group of knights?
Pick one rule. What do you think it was meant to teach the brothers about how to live?
Why might a group choose this picture as its symbol? Give one idea about what it could mean.
What do the arrows show? How did houses far from Jerusalem help the knights there?
Which traveler would a robber notice first? What must the second traveler trust for her plan to work?
Which building is the oldest? About how many years apart are the oldest and the newest?

l.t: A Famous Monk Cheers Them On
l.look: Bernard was a supporter of the Templars. How might that change the way he described them?
The two writers lived about 40 years apart. How could both be telling part of the truth?

ch.bq: How do historians use old records to sort what really happened to the Templars from the legends told later?
ch.talk: Why might an important paper stay lost for hundreds of years, even inside a library?
ch.story: The Parchment in the Wrong Place

l.look: Put these facts together. What reasons might Philip have had to turn against the Templars? Which fact seems most important to you?
Find the loaded words. How do they want the reader to feel? Does the opening show any proof?
Is the boy's first answer strong evidence? What would you want to find before deciding what really happened?
About how many brothers did the commission hear? Why might it help to have so many voices, and not just one?
The cardinals forgave the leaders. Does that mean the pope thought the whole order was innocent? What else would you want to know?
About how many years passed between writing the parchment and finding it again?
How is the headline different from the document? Rewrite the headline so it matches the evidence.

Put the three events in order. How could these dates make people believe in a curse, even without proof?
Which claim is backed by records from the time? Which ones are legends? Tell what clue helped you decide.
Is your school team descended from real knights, or inspired by them? How is this like the Chicago Knights Templar of 1880?

6.bq: What did Americans gain by joining lodges and orders, and who had to build their own?
std: Describe individuals and groups who brought about important historical change
SS.CV.3.4
Identify civic virtues and democratic principles that guide Illinois and the nation
Identify local problems and some of the ways people are working to address them
6.write: Why did people build their own lodges and orders? Choose two groups from this unit, such as African Lodge and the Knights of Columbus. Use at least two facts or sources from the unit to explain what each group gave its members.

ch.bq: How did Prince Hall use a lodge, a pen and his voice to help his community?
ch.talk: Why do you think Prince Hall used the Revolution's own ideas about freedom in his petition?

l.look: Which claim is more careful? What word in it shows that the writer is not sure?
How many men were made Masons in all, counting Prince Hall? Why might joining as a group matter to them?
What could your club still do without the paper? What would change once the school signed it?
How many years passed between the charter being signed and it reaching Boston?
Which person did Alleyne study to learn about the date? Why would that person's records help?

s.t: Speaking Up for Freedom and School

l.look: What reason did the signers give for freedom? Find one idea that matches the Declaration of Independence.
Why did the parents think the rule was unfair? Use the word taxes in your answer.

Which Illinois city had the first lodge on this list? How many years later was the Grand Lodge formed?
How is this like the story of Prince Hall lodges? What finally changed in 1989?
About how many years do the papers cover? Why might a long span help a historian?

ch.bq: Why did so many Americans join lodges and orders, and what did they get from belonging?
ch.talk: What did Karl get from his lodge while he was alive? What did his family get after he died?

l.look: If a street had 30 grown men, about how many would belong to a lodge by Beito's estimate?
How is the class jar like a lodge's mutual aid? Why does it work better when many people join?
Which order used this symbol? What does each letter stand for?

l.t: The Order of the Eastern Star
l.look: Why might a group teach its values through stories instead of a list of rules?
What problem does this man have? How did Father McGivney try to solve it?
Which order on this list is oldest? How many years after the Odd Fellows did the Knights of Columbus begin?
What did a member have to do to get a monument? Why might this promise help the order find new members?
Does this program show a group hiding, or a group being public? What clue tells you?
How many years did the Masonic Temple stand? How many years apart were the two temples finished?
Which group lost the largest share of members? Which lost the smallest share?

7.bq: Why did secret societies hide their words in codes, and how do people unlock them?
std: Judge how useful a historical source is by its maker, date, origin, audience and purpose
Explain how documents, objects, pictures and oral accounts can be used to study the past
Find sources with multiple points of view to help answer essential questions
7.write: Why did secret societies hide their words in codes? Use the Leeson stone, the Copiale Cipher and the Schaw Statutes. Cite at least two facts from the unit, and explain how members and critics might see the same secret differently.

ch.t: Codes on Stones and in Books
ch.bq: How can a message be hidden in plain sight, and how do people figure out what it says?
ch.talk: Why do you think someone would carve a message in code on a gravestone, where anyone can see it?

l.look: Using the same grid, what shape would you draw for the letter C? Describe which sides have lines.

l.t: An Old Idea, a Masonic Name
l.look: Which claim fits the evidence of dates better? Explain how the dates help you decide.
Which message uses a code, and which uses a cipher? What clue helped you tell them apart?
Which parts of this stone could anyone understand, and which part needs a key? Explain.
Which letter shows up most in this short message? Why might that help a codebreaker who did not have the key?

l.t: Why Put Code on a Grave?
l.look: Which visitor uses evidence? Point to one fact each visitor gives or leaves out.
How many places did Caesar shift each letter? Use the clue about A and D to explain.
How many tries might the classmate need to find the key? What could Jada and Luis do to make their cipher harder to break?
About how many times more common is E than Z? What would you guess first if a symbol appeared a lot in a secret message?
What word might star, moon, box spell? Which three letters would you now know? Explain your thinking.

l.t: Make and Break a Code Together
l.look: What clue do you think Team Two will spot first? Name one short word or pattern that could give the message away.

ch.t: The Copiale Cipher and the Art of Memory
ch.bq: How do people and tools work together to unlock a secret, and how do people remember what they cannot write down?
ch.talk: The researchers lived in two different countries. How do you think that helped or made their work harder?

l.look: How many more symbols did the Copiale use than the English alphabet has letters? What might the extra symbols be for?
Which two Copiale tricks is Maria using? How would each trick slow down a codebreaker?
About how many years passed between when the Copiale was written and when it was cracked? Show how you figured it out.
What did the computer find? What must a person still do next? Name one job for each.
What two big facts did the team report? Why would other scientists want to read how they did it?
What job would you give each person? Which Copiale researcher is each one most like?
What does "see" mean in these sentences? How does this help explain why the Oculists used the eye as a symbol?
What is each speaker worried about or proud of? For the Copiale, what does the evidence show?
Who had to be tested, and what happened to a mason who failed? Why might a lodge care so much about memory?
Close your eyes and walk through the three spots. Can you name all three things? Which picture was easiest to remember, and why?
What five facts did you place, and where? Walk through your palace and say them aloud to a partner.

8.bq: How did working stonemasons become the Freemasons, and how can records help us sort true stories about them from legends?
std: SS.H.1.6-8.MdC
Analyze connections among events and developments within broader historical contexts
Classify the kinds of historical sources used in secondary interpretations
SS.CV.1.6-8.MdC
Describe how political, civil and economic organizations shape people's lives
8.write: A classmate says: "The Freemasons designed the United States, and the dollar bill proves it." Is this claim documented, disputed or unsupported? Use at least three facts or sources from this unit to explain your answer.

ch.t: Guilds, Lodges and the First Grand Lodge
ch.bq: How did groups of working stonemasons turn into a club of gentlemen, and how do we know?
ch.talk: Why might a single sentence in a diary be stronger evidence than a long story written a hundred years later?

l.look: Name two jobs the lodge hut did for these workers. Why would the name of the hut come to mean the group of people inside it?
Which of these rules would still make sense at a job today? Which one surprises you?

Which of your rules is most like Schaw's order to keep records? Why would that rule help historians hundreds of years later?
How many years passed between the Regius Poem and the oldest lodge minute? Which two papers are closest together in time?

l.t: The Mason Word and the Memory Test
l.look: Why would a trade with few written papers care so much about memory?
What does this entry prove for sure? What questions does it leave open?
Pick a tool from your own classroom. What idea could it stand for? Explain your choice.
How many years after 1717 was the 1717 story first printed? Why might that gap make a historian cautious?
Why might this rule have made it easier for men from different churches to meet as friends?
Why do groups like private traditions? How is a safe secret different from a secret that hides someone getting hurt?
What does each side worry about or value? Can both descriptions be partly true?

ch.bq: Which founders were really Masons, and how can the paper trail test a popular claim?
ch.talk: Before you read the chapter, what would you need to see to believe that Masons designed the eye on the dollar?

l.look: How did Franklin's view of the lodges seem to change in four years? What might explain the change?
Why is an account book written that same evening strong evidence that Washington joined?
How is this like the claim that Masons planned the Revolution because some patriots were Masons?
What two things does Adams say in this letter? Why is it hard to argue that he was secretly a Mason?
Which statement best matches the evidence in this lesson? What is wrong with each of the other two?
What does this letter tell you about how active Washington was in his lodge late in life?
How old was Washington, born in 1732, when he laid the Capitol cornerstone? How many years passed between joining and the cornerstone?

l.t: Was the Revolution a Masonic Plan?
l.look: Which facts might seem to support the claim of a Masonic plan? Which facts weaken it? What do you conclude?

l.t: A Seal for a New Nation
l.look: Where was the eye placed in this first design? Does the report say anything about Masons?
How many years passed between adopting the seal and putting it on the dollar? What does that gap tell you about who designed the eye?
Does this letter show that Masons designed the seal, or that Masons chose to put it on the dollar? Explain the difference.

l.t: Testing a Claim with the Paper Trail
l.look: Is Maya's answer fair to both sides? What source from this chapter would you add to make it stronger?

9.bq: What do societies with private knowledge do for their members, and how can outsiders study them fairly and respectfully?
std: Identify how cultural and environmental characteristics vary among world regions
SS.H.2.6-8.MdC
Analyze the many factors that shaped people's perspectives in different eras
Analyze how the outlook of source creators shaped what the historical record contains
9.write: Is 'secret society' a fair label for groups like Sande, Ekpe or the Heaven and Earth Society? Take a position. Use two or three facts or sources from this unit to support it, and explain one view that disagrees with yours.

ch.t: Poro, Sande and Ekpe in West Africa
ch.bq: How can outsiders learn about societies that keep some knowledge private, and still show them respect?
ch.talk: Why might a community want some of its teaching to stay private, even when the celebration is public?
ch.story: Coming Home from the Sande School

l.look: Both writers describe the same kind of group. Which words make it sound frightening? Which make it sound ordinary? Which description helps a reader more?
List two ways these events are alike and one way they are different. What does each community want its young people to feel?
According to this summary, did Poro replace the chiefs or work with them? Which words tell you?
Name the three occasions the label lists. Why would a museum point out that women danced this mask?
Pick one detail. What idea might it stand for? Use a clue from the reading to support your answer.
How many years did the civil war last? Which book came out while the war was going on?
Why is a diary written by an Ekpe member himself valuable evidence? What is one limit of evidence that survives only in excerpts?
Which record is oldest? How many years passed between Antera Duke's diary and Macgregor's list?
Why might these two writers see Abakuá so differently? What evidence would help you decide which description is closer to the truth?
Which of these would you use in a school report, and which would you leave out? Explain your reasons.
What does the title tell you about Harley's main idea? Whose point of view might be missing from a study written by an outsider?
Whose point of view does this book mainly show? What other voices would you want to hear before deciding what happened?

ch.bq: How can we tell a society's proud founding legend from what the records show, and why do both matter?
ch.talk: What does a person need most when they are far from home? How could a secret sign help meet that need?
ch.story: A Sign at the Tea Stall

l.look: List three things this man needs. For each one, who could help him if his family is far away?
What kind of evidence did these historians use? What do they say the society was NOT at first?

l.t: Help for Men on the Move
l.look: Which answer do Murray, Qin and Ownby favor for the early years? What kind of evidence would you need to support Answer A?
Why would a government official want to learn a society's recognition signs? How might his job shape what he wrote?
Why might a book built from seized papers be useful to historians today? Why might members have felt differently about it?
What does the visitor get right? What might he miss by comparing? How is this like Western writers who called the Hung League 'Chinese Freemasonry'?

l.look: What does each story say about the values of the group that tells it? Why might people keep telling a story even if no records prove it?
How many years separate the legend's date from the first date in the records? What might explain such a big gap?
Which source is better evidence for when the society began? Which is better evidence for what members believed? Explain your thinking.

l.t: When Some Branches Turned to Crime

Why might a city protect this building? What stories does it hold besides the 1988 raid?

Evaluate the powers and responsibilities of citizens, parties, interest groups and the media

10.write: Was the fear of secret societies between 1826 and 1913 mostly fair or mostly unfair? Choose one case from the unit. Cite two or three facts or sources, and explain your claim.

ch.bq: How did one man's disappearance in 1826 change the way Americans felt about secret societies and politics?
ch.talk: Why might a mystery with no clear answer make people angrier than a crime that is solved in court?

Compare the ways individuals and groups change society, promote the common good and protect rights
